strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful evaluation problem: determining how much microscopy benchmark performance requires learned representations. Competitive random-network baselines on RxRx3-core provide concrete motivation for including stronger controls when reporting foundation-model results.

Originality: The contribution is primarily diagnostic rather than architectural. Combining random encoders, pixel statistics, cell-centroid representations, layer-wise evaluation, and gene-wise comparisons offers a useful perspective across cellular and tissue imaging.

Soundness: Several observations receive substantial empirical support through multiple architectures, three initialization seeds, retrieval folds, and comparisons on both original and coarsened HEST data. Preserving patient-level splits when constructing overlapping HEST-1k-1NN patches is an appropriate safeguard.

Presentation and limitations: The discussion acknowledges important counterevidence, including stronger results from proprietary MAE embeddings and clear pretraining gains on JUMP-CP and HEST. It also explicitly recognizes that real-tissue structure results may be explained by cell count. These qualifications are valuable, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described use of existing datasets.
weaknesses: Soundness—central interpretation: Competitive random features establish that learning is unnecessary for some benchmark scores; they do not establish that trained models fail to acquire biologically meaningful features or exploit nonbiological shortcuts. Biological signal can itself be accessible through simple morphology or intensity features. Likewise, correlated similarity rankings do not identify the underlying cues, and weak improvements across layers do not demonstrate the absence of abstraction. The manuscript lacks controlled interventions or direct biological probes sufficient to support its stronger claims.

Significance and claim calibration: The abstract's broad statement that state-of-the-art methods perform comparably to the baselines overstates the findings. Section 4.1 reports approximately 1.5-fold higher average recall from MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8, while pretrained models consistently outperform random baselines on JUMP-CP. In Table 1, in-domain tissue models outperform structural baselines on all four displayed datasets. These results support task-dependent limitations and better benchmark calibration more convincingly than a general failure of current representation learning.

Soundness—structural interpretation: Cell-centroid baselines retain meaningful biology and depend on a pretrained CellViT segmenter. Their success cannot by itself establish shortcut learning by image encoders. Moreover, Table 6 shows that cell count nearly matches GCN performance on PRAD and COAD: 0.37 versus 0.38 and 0.30 versus 0.31, respectively. The acknowledged absence of count-controlled real-tissue experiments leaves the added contribution of spatial arrangement unresolved; synthetic classification does not resolve that attribution.

Reproducibility: Although model identifiers and benchmark references are supplied, important details of the custom pipeline remain unspecified. These include the precise negative-control batch correction, image intensity preprocessing, RxRx3 subsampling and quality-control selections, and the exact ViT channel-expansion procedure. SingleConv's configuration and synthetic-model training hyperparameters are also insufficiently documented, and no implementation repository for this study is provided. These omissions matter because preprocessing can substantially affect random-feature retrieval.

Evaluation reliability: Table 1 reports best-in-class results, and Appendix D.1 explicitly selects the best cell-count configuration per dataset, without clearly describing independent validation for these choices. This makes selected comparisons susceptible to optimistic selection. Several highlighted tissue datasets contain only two patients (Table 2), limiting the strength of generalization claims. Fold standard deviations and initialization stability do not establish statistical equivalence between trained and untrained representations.

Presentation: The paper is generally organized clearly, but some reporting needs reconciliation. Table 1 says its best structural models were pretrained on natural images, whereas its PRAD, SKCM, and COAD structural scores coincide with the synthetic-pretrained GCN results in Table 6. Several central figures also have very small legends. More explicit configuration attribution and readily readable quantitative comparisons would make the conclusions easier to audit.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses an important evaluation problem: how much microscopy benchmark performance requires learned representations. Competitive random-network and pixel-statistics baselines on RxRx3-core provide useful reference points for interpreting foundation-model scores.

Originality: The contribution lies in empirical understanding rather than a new architecture. Combining random encoders, layer-wise analyses, cell-centroid representations, and gene-wise comparisons offers a useful diagnostic perspective across cellular and tissue imaging.

Soundness: The evaluation includes multiple architectures, three initialization seeds for cellular baselines, detailed per-dataset results, and both original and coarsened HEST benchmarks. Appendix B explicitly preserves patient-level splits despite overlapping tissue patches, addressing an important leakage concern.

Presentation and limitations: The main narrative is accessible, and the discussion acknowledges that prediction alignment does not establish mechanism and that tissue structure may primarily encode cell count. Reporting positive results for pretraining, including proprietary-model embeddings, is valuable. The use of existing datasets raises no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—central inference exceeds the evidence: Competitive random features establish that some benchmark signal is accessible without representation learning; they do not establish that trained models lack biologically meaningful features or exploit acquisition artifacts. Biological effects can themselves produce simple intensity, density, or morphological changes. Likewise, Spearman correlations of approximately 0.68–0.80 across all gene-pair similarities do not demonstrate identical mechanisms or equivalent retrieval of biologically relevant pairs. Direct nuisance-controlled tests or biological concept probes are needed to support the abstract's stronger claims.

Significance and scope—the headline underrepresents substantial gains from learning: Section 4.1 reports that pretrained models consistently outperform untrained baselines on JUMP-CP and that MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8 reach approximately 1.5 times higher average recall on balanced RxRx3-core. Table 1 also shows clear in-domain advantages across all four displayed tissue categories, including 0.68 versus 0.45 for the best structural baseline on SKCM. These findings support task-dependent benefits of learning more strongly than the abstract's broad statement that state-of-the-art methods perform comparably to simple baselines.

Reproducibility—important parts of the cellular pipeline remain underspecified: Appendix B mentions negative controls for batch-effect mitigation without specifying the transformation and fitting procedure. Image intensity normalization, exact subsample/fold membership, the SingleConv configuration, and details of the custom ViT channel-expansion scheme are insufficiently documented. No implementation repository for this study is identified. These omissions matter particularly when interpreting low-level cues, representation collapse, and pretrained-versus-random comparisons.

Soundness—tissue structure is not cleanly separated from cell count or learned preprocessing: Centroids come from pretrained CellViT, so the structure pipeline already incorporates learned image analysis. Table 6 shows that cell count nearly matches GCN on PRAD and COAD, leaving the incremental contribution of arrangement unresolved. The synthetic experiment does not fully resolve this: Table 4 assigns different counts to several classes, despite the stated aim of controlling count. The authors appropriately acknowledge the real-data limitation, but the stronger interpretation still needs count-matched controls.

Evaluation reliability: Several tissue categories contain only two patients (Table 2), limiting confidence in broad generalization. Table 1 reports best-in-class results, and Appendix D.1 selects the best cell-count feature configuration per dataset, without a clearly documented independent selection protocol. Fold standard deviations alone do not resolve selection bias or establish equivalence between models. The eight positive-control compounds in JUMP-CP also provide a narrow basis for conclusions about cell-culture representations generally.

Presentation—material inconsistencies impede verification: Table 1 describes the structural winners as pretrained on natural images, but its PRAD, SKCM, and COAD values match the synthetically pretrained GCN in Tables 6–7. Table 6 reports SKCM cell-count performance of 0.40, whereas Table 7 assigns 0.32 to PCA-plus-ridge and 0.40 to XGBoost, despite the stated main-text preference for ridge. Figure 3 labels mAP as recall, and Figure 23 describes JUMP-CP results as ImageNet retrieval. These should be reconciled before the results can serve as a reliable benchmarking reference.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful question: what do microscopy benchmark scores actually establish? Competitive random-network, pixel-statistic, and cell-count baselines provide practical reference points for interpreting representation learning results.

Originality: The contribution lies in empirical understanding rather than architectural novelty. Combining layer-wise analysis, gene-pair ranking comparisons, and tissue representations based on cell positions offers complementary diagnostics across two biological imaging scales.

Soundness: Several descriptive findings are well supported. Appendix G examines three random initializations; tissue evaluation preserves patient-level splits; and the appendices evaluate both original and coarsened HEST benchmarks. The compound-specific results also reveal informative variation hidden by aggregate scores.

Presentation and limitations: The discussion acknowledges clear gains from in-domain pretraining, the strong proprietary-model embeddings, and the unresolved distinction between cell count and spatial arrangement. These qualifications are valuable. The study uses existing datasets, and no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central interpretation: Competitive random features establish that these tasks can be solved partly without learned representations; they do not establish that trained models lack biologically meaningful features or exploit technical shortcuts. Simple intensity and density measurements can themselves contain real biology. Likewise, correlated similarity rankings and flat layer-wise performance do not identify the information a model uses. The stronger claims require direct biological probes or interventions separating biological signal from acquisition confounders.

Scope of conclusions: The abstract's broad characterization of state-of-the-art methods as comparable to simple baselines understates contrary evidence. Section 4.1 reports approximately 1.5-fold higher recall for MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8, pretrained models consistently improve JUMP-CP retrieval, and Table 1 shows substantial in-domain advantages across all four reported tissue categories. The supported conclusion is more specific: simple baselines contextualize particular benchmarks and model families.

Reproducibility: Important custom pipeline details remain unspecified, including fluorescence preprocessing, feature post-processing and DMSO-based batch correction, exact sampled image/plate identities, and the custom ViT channel-expansion procedure. No implementation repository for this study is provided. References to existing evaluation pipelines do not fully specify these modifications, which are particularly consequential for a study about low-level cues and batch effects.

Tissue interpretation: Cell-centroid representations depend on pretrained CellViT segmentation and therefore are not independent of learned image processing. Their additional information beyond cell count also remains uncertain: Table 6 reports closely matched GCN and cell-count scores on PRAD and COAD. The acknowledged need for count-conditioned real-tissue analysis limits the stronger interpretation of spatial organization as a distinct explanatory signal.

Evaluation and presentation: Several tissue subsets contain only two patients, and best-in-class/configuration selection lacks a clearly stated independent validation procedure. Fold variability therefore does not establish robust equivalence between models. Reporting also needs correction: Figure 3 labels mAP as recall, Figure 23 describes compound retrieval as ImageNet retrieval, and Table 1 describes structure-model pretraining as natural-image training despite several scores matching the synthetic-pretrained GCN in Table 6. These issues impede reliable interpretation and reuse.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful evaluation problem: how much microscopy benchmark performance actually requires learned representations. The RxRx3-core comparison is informative: an untrained ViT achieves 0.19±0.02 recall versus 0.20±0.02 for OpenPhenom, with pixel statistics reaching 0.16±0.02 (Table 13). These results justify routinely including stronger simple baselines.

Originality: The contribution is primarily empirical understanding rather than a new architecture. Combining random encoders, intermediate-layer probes, gene-pair ranking comparisons, and cell-centroid representations across cellular and tissue tasks provides a useful diagnostic perspective.

Soundness: The study includes several valuable checks: multiple random initializations, architecture and pooling sweeps, evaluation on the original and coarsened HEST benchmarks, and patient-stratified HEST splits. Reporting results on the original full RxRx3-core dataset also helps contextualize the subsampled experiments.

Presentation and limitations: The main narrative is accessible, and the appendices provide extensive results. The authors explicitly acknowledge that prediction alignment does not establish shortcut use, that tissue structure may largely proxy cell count, and that stronger proprietary models outperform the baselines. These acknowledgments appropriately qualify the findings.

Research ethics: The study uses existing public datasets and models or released embeddings, and its impact statement recognizes the need to validate biological predictions. No material ethical concern is apparent from the reported work.
weaknesses: Soundness—central interpretation exceeds the evidence. Competitive random features establish that learning is unnecessary for some measured performance; they do not establish that trained models lack biological abstractions or exploit spurious signals. Intensity, cell count, and spatial organization can themselves encode genuine biology. Likewise, correlated rankings in Figure 3 do not identify the features responsible. The stronger claims in the abstract and Sections 5.2 and 7 require controlled interventions or confounder-conditioned evaluations, or should be narrowed to benchmark discrimination.

Soundness—the ImageNet comparison does not isolate biological abstraction. Many reference backbones were trained directly on ImageNet labels, whereas microscopy evaluation involves domain transfer, different downstream metrics, and custom multichannel adaptation. Flat layer-wise retrieval curves can reflect these differences or probe limitations. Section B.5 also uses different channel-expansion treatments for ViTs and ResNets, without a sensitivity analysis, complicating architectural interpretations.

Significance and scope: The strongest in-domain results substantially qualify the headline. MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8 achieve approximately 1.5 times higher average RxRx3-core recall, pretrained models consistently improve JUMP-CP retrieval, and histology foundation models show clear HEST gains. These findings support a narrower conclusion about particular models and tasks. The eight-control-compound JUMP experiment also provides limited coverage of the broader perturbation space.

Soundness of tissue conclusions: Structure-only inputs depend on a pretrained CellViT segmenter and therefore are information-restricted representations, not an entirely uninformed pipeline. Table 2 shows that cell count nearly matches GCN performance on PRAD and COAD. Synthetic demonstrations of arrangement sensitivity do not establish its contribution on real tissue. Furthermore, HEST-1k-1NN simultaneously changes spatial context, effective image resolution, and target smoothing; these effects are not separately controlled.

Statistical reliability and model selection: Several highlighted HEST subsets contain only two patients (Table 3), limiting generalization despite numerous patches. Results repeatedly select the best configuration, including cell-count transformations and aggregation strategies, without clearly specifying an independent selection procedure. Fold standard deviations alone do not resolve selection optimism or establish practical equivalence between models.

Reproducibility and presentation: The stated code release points to an empty footnote on page 9, leaving no usable repository link in the manuscript. Important implementation details remain incomplete, including the SingleConv configuration, exact custom channel expansion, and end-to-end normalization and aggregation settings. There are also reporting inconsistencies: Figure 5 labels its vertical axis 'Recall' although it reports mAP, and Table 1 describes the best structure models as natural-image pretrained although its scores align with the synthetic-pretrained GCN in Table 2. These issues impede reliable reuse.

strengths: Significance: The paper provides useful calibration of microscopy benchmarks with pixel statistics, random encoders, and tissue-structure baselines. On RxRx3-core, Table 13 reports recall of 0.19±0.02 for an untrained ViT versus 0.20±0.02 for OpenPhenom, supporting the practical recommendation to include strong simple baselines.

Soundness: The empirical investigation spans several tasks and includes initialization checks, layer-wise analyses, retrieval-ranking comparisons, and both original and coarsened HEST evaluations. Patient-stratified HEST splits appropriately prevent leakage from overlapping spatial patches.

Originality: The contribution lies primarily in comparative understanding rather than architectural novelty. Combining random-feature diagnostics with centroid-only tissue representations provides a useful perspective on what different evaluations reward.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript acknowledges results favoring pretrained models, including JUMP-CP, histology foundation models, and proprietary MAE embeddings. Sections 5.4 and 6 explicitly distinguish unresolved causal questions from observations. The use of public datasets and the stated impact discussion raise no material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—central interpretation: Competitive random features establish that learning is unnecessary for some measured performance, but do not establish that the predictive signal is biologically meaningless or spurious. Intensity, cell abundance, and tissue organization can themselves reflect genuine biology. Likewise, correlated retrieval rankings and flat layer-wise curves do not demonstrate that models exploit the same mechanisms or lack high-level abstractions. The stronger claims in Sections 5.1–5.2 require controlled interventions or narrower wording.

Significance and scope: The strongest conclusions about benchmark inadequacy are qualified by the paper’s own positive results. Section 4.1 reports approximately 1.5-fold higher recall for large in-domain MAEs, while Table 1 shows substantial gains from histology pretraining. These benchmarks therefore do discriminate some stronger representations. The paper should distinguish particular models failing to improve from an evaluation failing to measure useful progress.

Soundness—structure analysis: Centroids are extracted using pretrained CellViT, so the structure pipeline already incorporates learned image processing. Furthermore, Table 2 shows that cell count alone nearly matches the GCN on PRAD and COAD. Synthetic experiments establish representational capacity but do not identify what drives real-tissue predictions. The honest discussion of this limitation is welcome; nevertheless, evidence for useful spatial organization beyond count remains incomplete.

Evaluation uncertainty: Several highlighted HEST subsets contain only two patients (Table 3), limiting population-level conclusions despite many patches. Best-in-class results and per-dataset choices of cell-count features are reported without a clear independent selection protocol. JUMP-MoA matching differences are also reported without uncertainty. These issues weaken claims of parity or superiority.

Reproducibility and presentation: The code-release statement on page 9 has a footnote marker but no usable repository address. Important implementation choices, including the custom multichannel ViT expansion and precise preprocessing configuration, are insufficiently specified for independent reconstruction. Figure 5 labels its vertical axis 'Recall' although the text and caption describe mAP. Overall, the descriptive findings have clear merit, but the interpretation and evaluation documentation need revision before the broader conclusions are reliable.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful evaluation problem: how much microscopy benchmark performance requires learned representations. On RxRx3-core, an untrained ViT achieves recall@5% of 0.19±0.02 versus OpenPhenom's 0.20±0.02 (Table 13), making a compelling case for reporting stronger baseline comparisons.

Soundness: The empirical investigation spans cell-culture retrieval, spatial transcriptomics, and cancer subtyping, with layer-wise analyses, initialization checks, and per-compound/per-gene breakdowns. Patient-stratified HEST evaluation and reporting both original and coarsened benchmarks are valuable methodological choices.

Originality: The contribution is primarily new empirical understanding rather than a new architecture. Combining random features, pixel statistics, cell counts, and cell-centroid representations provides a useful framework for examining what information suffices for each task.

Presentation and limitations: The paper is generally well organized and acknowledges important counterevidence, including strong MAE-L/G results and clear benefits from in-domain pretraining. Sections 5.4 and 6 appropriately acknowledge that prediction alignment does not establish shortcut use and that tissue arrangement has not been separated from cell count. The public-data evaluation presents no evident material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—central interpretation: Competitive random-feature performance establishes that learning is unnecessary for some measured signal; it does not establish that this signal is biologically meaningless or spurious. Intensity, cell count, and tissue organization can themselves reflect real biology. Likewise, correlated similarity rankings do not show that trained and untrained models exploit 'essentially the same' features (Section 5.2). The abstract's claim that benchmarks mask a lack of relevant abstractions therefore exceeds the evidence. Controlled nuisance interventions or more narrowly stated conclusions are needed.

Soundness—layer-wise comparison: Increasing performance with depth is not a validated test for biological abstraction. Several ImageNet reference networks were trained directly on ImageNet classification, whereas microscopy evaluations involve different objectives, modalities, and aggregation pipelines. Consequently, contrasting their depth trends cannot isolate a distinctive failure of biological representation learning.

Significance and scope: The strongest evaluated cell-culture models, MAE-L/8 and MAE-G/8, outperform the baselines substantially—approximately 1.5-fold in averaged recall according to Section 4.1. In-domain models also clearly improve JUMP-CP and HEST performance. These findings support model- and task-specific diagnostics more strongly than a general failure of benchmark discrimination. Restricting JUMP-CP to eight controls further limits the breadth of that conclusion.

Statistical support: Several highlighted HEST subsets have only two patients (Table 3), limiting population-level interpretation despite numerous patches and genes. Best-performing configurations are reported repeatedly, and Appendix C.1 explicitly selects cell-count feature configurations per dataset without establishing independent validation selection. Paired uncertainty estimates and a clearly separated selection protocol would strengthen claims of comparable performance; Table 14 also lacks uncertainty estimates.

Reproducibility and presentation: The code-release statement points to an empty footnote on page 9, leaving no usable repository link in the manuscript. Important details remain incomplete, including SingleConv configuration, synthetic-model training hyperparameters, and the precise custom channel-expansion implementation. Figure 5 labels its vertical axis 'Recall' while the text and caption specify mAP. These issues impede reliable reproduction of the central comparisons.
